cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following conditions yields the optimum concentration of ammonia ($$NH_3$$) in the industrial Haber-Bosch process?

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the Haber process reaction**
$$N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$$, which is exothermic ($$\Delta H = -92\text{ kJ/mol}$$).
**Step 2: Apply Le Chatelier's Principle**
Since there are $$4\text{ moles}$$ of reactant gas and $$2\text{ moles}$$ of product gas, high pressure ($$200\text{ atm}$$) shifts equilibrium to the right.
Since the reaction is exothermic, low temperature shifts it right, but slows the rate.
**Step 3: Choose the compromise**
Industry uses about 200 atm and a moderate temperature of about 450 °C with an iron catalyst: a reasonable yield obtained at a fast enough rate.

cards.answer: High pressure (about 200 atm) and a moderate temperature (about 450 °C) with an iron catalyst

options.A: They are poor conductors of heat and electricity
options.D: They lose electrons to form positive ions

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Non-metals have no free electrons, so they conduct heat and electricity poorly (graphite is the exception).

**Step 2:** They are brittle when solid, form acidic or neutral oxides, and gain or share electrons.

**Step 3:** Answer: poor conductors.

**Tip:** Remember graphite as the classic exception – a non-metal that conducts electricity.

cards.title: Nonmetals: general properties
body: Nonmetals are on the right of the periodic table. Most are poor conductors of heat and electricity (graphite is an exception), are brittle when solid, have low melting points (diamond and graphite are exceptions with very high melting points), and tend to gain electrons to form negative ions or share electrons in covalent bonds. Their oxides are usually acidic (e.g. CO₂, SO₂).

cards.title: 3.2.1 Carbon
body: Carbon is found in all living things, both plants and animals.
Carbon occurs both in a free and in a combined state.

In its combined state carbon exists as carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, carbonates such as calcium carbonate, and in large quantities as organic compounds, such as hydrocarbons, oils, carbohydrates and proteins.
Allotropes are different forms of the same element that have different physical properties, but generally have the same chemical properties.

cards.title: The allotropes of carbon, step by step
body: **Allotropes** are different forms of the same element in the same physical state, with different structures and so different physical properties, but the same chemical properties (all three burn to CO₂). Carbon has three main crystalline allotropes: **diamond, graphite and fullerene**; charcoal, soot and coke are amorphous forms.

**Diamond:** every carbon atom forms **4 strong covalent bonds** to 4 other carbons arranged **tetrahedrally** (109.5°). The bonding continues in all directions → a **giant 3-D covalent network**. All 4 outer electrons are used in bonds.

**Graphite:** every carbon forms **3 covalent bonds** in a flat sheet of **hexagons** (120°). The 4th electron of each atom is **delocalised** (free to move along the sheet). The sheets (layers) are held together only by **weak forces**, so they slide over each other.

**Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀:** discovered in 1985. 60 carbon atoms form a hollow ball of **12 pentagons and 20 hexagons**, like a football (“buckyball”). Each C bonds to 3 others. It is a **molecule**, not a giant structure — so it is much softer and dissolves in some organic solvents (e.g. benzene, giving a purple solution).

cards.title: Diamond: giant 3-D network
body: Every atom is joined to four others. There are no weak links and no free electrons.

cards.title: Graphite: layers of hexagons
body: Strong bonds inside each layer, weak forces between the layers.

cards.title: Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀
body: A closed cage of 60 atoms: 12 pentagons (one is shaded) surrounded by hexagons.

cards.title: Structure → property: the reasoning chain
body: **Hardness:** diamond has strong bonds in every direction → nothing can slide → very hard. Graphite’s layers are joined only by weak forces → layers slide → soft and slippery.
**Conductivity:** graphite has a delocalised electron on every atom that can move along the layers → conducts. Diamond’s electrons are all locked in bonds → insulator.
**Melting point:** to melt diamond or graphite you must break strong **covalent** bonds → both very high. C₆₀ molecules are held by weak forces between molecules → much lower.
Use this chain in every “explain” question: **structure → bonding → property**.

cards.title: Worked example: why does graphite conduct but diamond does not?
cards.problem: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not, although both are pure carbon.

steps.text: Electricity needs charged particles that can move.
Diamond: each C uses all 4 outer electrons in 4 covalent bonds → no free electrons → non-conductor.
Graphite: each C uses only 3 electrons in bonds; the 4th is delocalised along the layer.
These delocalised electrons move when a voltage is applied → graphite conducts (along the layers).

cards.answer: Graphite has delocalised electrons; diamond has none.

cards.title: Worked example: high melting point but soft?
cards.problem: Graphite has a higher melting point than diamond but is very soft. How can both be true?

steps.text: Melting graphite means breaking the strong covalent bonds **within** the layers → very high melting point.
Softness depends on the **weak forces between** the layers, which let the layers slide (pencil marks, lubricant).
So different forces control the two properties.

cards.answer: Strong bonds inside layers (high m.p.); weak forces between layers (soft).

cards.title: Memory trick
body: **Diamond = 4 = Fixed** (all electrons in bonds: hard, no current). **Graphite = 3 + 1 free** (layers slide, electrons flow). **C₆₀ = football** (12 pentagons + 20 hexagons).

cards.title: 3.2.2 Carbon Monoxide
body: Industrially carbon monoxide is manufactured by passing carbon dioxide gas over red-hot charcoal at a temperature about 1000°C.
The concentrated sulphuric acid removes water from the formic acid resulting in the production of carbon monoxide.
**Carbon monoxide** is a good reducing agent because it removes oxygen during the reaction with reactive metal oxides.
For example, lead oxide is reduced to lead.

cards.title: 3.2.3 Carbon Dioxide
body: **Carbon dioxide** is a colourless gas present in the air at about 0.04 % by volume (it was about 0.03 % fifty years ago).
Human beings inhale oxygen from the air and exhale carbon dioxide.
During photosynthesis, plants use carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and give off oxygen.
**Carbon dioxide** is an important chemical link between the plant and the animal world.

cards.title: Carbonic acid, step by step
body: **Formation:** carbon dioxide dissolves slightly in water and some of it reacts: CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq). Carbonic acid exists **only in solution**; it is **weak** and **unstable** — warming or opening a soft-drink bottle drives the CO₂ out.
**Weak acid:** only a small fraction ionises, so it turns blue litmus red **slowly** and only faintly.
**Dibasic (diprotic):** it has two replaceable H and ionises in two steps:
$$\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{HCO}_3^- \qquad \text{HCO}_3^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{CO}_3^{2-}$$
**Two series of salts:** **hydrogen carbonates** (acid salts, HCO₃⁻), e.g. NaHCO₃, and **carbonates** (normal salts, CO₃²⁻), e.g. Na₂CO₃, CaCO₃.

**Solubility and heat:** Na and K carbonates dissolve in water and are **not** decomposed by heat. Carbonates of Ca, Mg, Zn, Cu … are insoluble and decompose on heating: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). Hydrogen carbonates decompose easily: 2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(g) + CO₂(g) (why baking soda makes dough rise).

**Everyday links:** soda water and soft drinks; normal rain is slightly acidic (pH ≈ 5.6) because of dissolved CO₂; rain with CO₂ slowly dissolves limestone: CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → Ca(HCO₃)₂ (caves, temporary hardness of water).

cards.title: Worked example: CO₂ into sodium hydroxide
cards.problem: Carbon dioxide is bubbled into sodium hydroxide solution, first a little, then in excess. Write the equations.

steps.text: Little CO₂ (NaOH in excess) → the normal salt: 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O
Excess CO₂ → the acid salt: Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → 2NaHCO₃
Overall with excess CO₂: NaOH + CO₂ → NaHCO₃

cards.answer: Na₂CO₃ first, then NaHCO₃ with excess CO₂ — two salts because H₂CO₃ is dibasic.

cards.title: Worked example: the limewater test
cards.problem: Explain why limewater turns milky with CO₂ and then clears again if CO₂ is bubbled for a long time.

steps.text: Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution.
CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O: insoluble white CaCO₃ makes it **milky**.
Excess CO₂: CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → Ca(HCO₃)₂, which is **soluble** → the solution clears.

cards.why: H₂CO₃ can lose one H (→ HCO₃⁻, acid salts) or both (→ CO₃²⁻, normal salts).

cards.title: Tips
body: Write carbonic acid formation with ⇌: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ (it is reversible and unstable).
Acid salt = still has replaceable H (NaHCO₃); normal salt = all H replaced (Na₂CO₃).
Higher in the activity series → more stable carbonate.

cards.title: The carbon cycle, step by step
body: Carbon is in every living thing. It moves between the **air**, **living things**, the **oceans** and **rocks and fuels**, and carbon dioxide is the “transfer agent” that carries it. The **carbon cycle** is the set of processes that keeps the CO₂ in the air (about 0.04 % by volume) roughly constant.
**Step 1 — Photosynthesis removes CO₂.** Green plants use sunlight and chlorophyll to turn CO₂ and water into glucose and oxygen:
$$6\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)} + 6\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \xrightarrow{\text{sunlight},\ \text{chlorophyll}} \mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6}(aq)} + 6\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}$$
**Step 2 — Feeding passes carbon on.** Animals eat plants (and other animals); the carbon becomes part of their bodies.
**Step 3 — Respiration returns CO₂.** Plants and animals oxidise glucose to release energy:
$$\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6}(aq)} + 6\mathrm{O_{2}(g)} \rightarrow 6\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)} + 6\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \qquad \text{energy released}$$
**Step 4 — Decay returns CO₂.** When plants and animals die, bacteria and fungi (decomposers) break them down and respire, releasing CO₂.
**Step 5 — Fossil fuels store carbon.** Remains buried for millions of years without air become coal, oil and natural gas.

**Step 6 — Combustion returns CO₂ fast.** Burning fuels, wood and charcoal: \(\mathrm{CH_{4}(g)} + 2\mathrm{O_{2}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}\), \(\mathrm{C(s)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}\).

**Step 7 — Oceans and rocks.** CO₂ dissolves in rain water and in the oceans: \(\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_{2}CO_{3}(aq)}\). Sea animals use dissolved carbonate to build shells of CaCO₃, which become limestone. Heating limestone and volcanoes release CO₂ again.

**Correction:** the textbook says CO₂ is removed “as acid rain”. CO₂ makes rain water only **very slightly acidic** (pH ≈ 5.6); “acid rain” means rain made much more acidic by SO₂ and nitrogen oxides. The correct statement is that CO₂ **dissolves in rain, seas and oceans**.

steps.text: **Photosynthesis** takes CO₂ out of the air into plants.
**Respiration and decay** put CO₂ back into the air.
**Combustion** of fossil fuels and wood puts back CO₂ that was stored for millions of years.
**Oceans** dissolve CO₂ (H₂CO₃, carbonates, limestone) and release it again.

cards.title: Upsetting the balance: the greenhouse effect
body: **Step 1:** sunlight warms the Earth's surface. **Step 2:** the warm surface gives out **infrared** radiation. **Step 3:** CO₂ (and methane, water vapour) absorbs infrared and acts like a **thermal blanket**.
**Step 4:** human activities add CO₂ faster than plants and oceans can remove it — **burning fossil fuels** and **cutting down forests** (fewer trees for photosynthesis, and the wood is often burnt).
**Result:** more CO₂ → stronger greenhouse effect → **global warming** → changed rainfall, droughts, melting ice and rising sea levels.
**What helps:** planting trees, using less fuel, renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro), efficient stoves.
**Do not confuse:** the greenhouse effect is about CO₂ trapping heat; the **ozone hole** is caused by CFCs; **acid rain** is caused by SO₂ and NOₓ.

cards.title: Worked example: CO₂ from burning charcoal
cards.problem: Calculate the mass of CO₂ produced when 1.2 kg of charcoal (pure carbon) burns completely. (C = 12, O = 16)

steps.text: $$\mathrm{C(s)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}$$
1 mol C (12 g) gives 1 mol CO₂ (44 g).
The mass is larger than the charcoal because oxygen from the air is added.

cards.title: Worked example: CO₂ used in photosynthesis
cards.problem: What mass of CO₂ must a plant take in to make 90 g of glucose? (C₆H₁₂O₆ = 180 g/mol)

steps.text: $$6\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)} + 6\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6}(aq)} + 6\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}$$
\(n(\text{glucose}) = 90/180 = 0.50\ \text{mol}\)
Ratio 6 : 1 → \(n(\text{CO}_2) = 3.0\ \text{mol}\); \(m = 3.0 \times 44 = 132\ \text{g}\).

cards.title: 3.3.1 Nitrogen
body: Nitrogen is also a constituent element of plant and animal proteins and nucleic acids.
Nitrogen may be obtained in the laboratory by heating a mixture of ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) and sodium nitrite.
The ammonium nitrite that is formed in this reaction is very unstable and is decomposed into water and nitrogen by gentle heating.
Since, nitrogen has a low boiling point, then it is recovered as a gas at the top of the fractionating column.

cards.title: 3.3.2 Ammonia
body: Small quantities of ammonia are found in the atmosphere, in barns, toilets, dung and in the soil.
When an animal and vegetable matter decomposed, much of the protein present in these substances is converted to ammonia.
Nitrogen from the air and hydrogen from natural gas are mixed in the ration of 1:3 by volume.
Nitrogen and hydrogen react at a high temperature and pressure over an iron catalyst.

cards.title: 3.3.3 Nitric Acid and its Compounds
body: Nitric acid is one of the most important inorganic acids.
Laboratory preparation of nitric acid Nitric acid is prepared by heating mixtures of sodium nitrate or potassium nitrate and concentrated sulphuric acid.
The mixture is heated gently and the gaseous nitric acid is given off as a gas.
Pure nitric acid is colourless, but the yellow colour of the distilled nitric acid is due to the dissolved nitrogen dioxide, a reddish brown gas, in the acid.

cards.title: The nitrogen cycle, step by step
body: Plants and animals need nitrogen to make **proteins**. Air is 78 % nitrogen, but N₂ has a very strong triple bond (N≡N), so most living things **cannot use N₂ directly**. Nitrogen must first be **fixed** — changed into ammonium or nitrate compounds.

**Step 1 — Nitrogen fixation (N₂ → compounds).** (a) **Nitrogen-fixing bacteria**, some free in the soil and some in the **root nodules of legumes** (beans, peas, clover, chickpeas), turn N₂ into ammonium compounds. (b) **Lightning** makes N₂ and O₂ combine; the oxides dissolve in rain to form nitric acid, which reaches the soil as nitrates:
$$\mathrm{N_{2}(g)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} \xrightarrow{\text{lightning}} 2\mathrm{NO(g)}$$
$$2\mathrm{NO(g)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NO_{2}(g)}$$
$$4\mathrm{NO_{2}(g)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{HNO_{3}(aq)}$$
(c) **Industry (Haber process)** makes ammonia for fertilisers: \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_{2}(g)} \overset{\text{Fe},\ \text{450}{}^{\circ}\text{C}}{\rightleftharpoons} 2\mathrm{NH_{3}(g)}\).
**Step 2 — Nitrification.** **Nitrifying bacteria** in the soil oxidise ammonium to nitrite and then to nitrate: NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻.
**Step 3 — Assimilation.** Plant roots absorb nitrates (and ammonium) and make **plant proteins**. Animals get nitrogen by **eating** plants.

**Step 4 — Ammonification (decay).** Dead plants and animals, urine and droppings are broken down by **decomposers** (bacteria and fungi); the nitrogen in proteins becomes **ammonia / ammonium** again.
**Step 5 — Denitrification.** **Denitrifying bacteria**, mainly in waterlogged soils with little air, turn nitrates back into **N₂ gas**, which returns to the air. The cycle is complete.

**Correction:** the textbook says that when plants and animals die, “denitrifying bacteria convert the nitrogen in the proteins” into atmospheric nitrogen, and that “some plants” convert N₂. Proteins are first turned into ammonium by **decomposers**; denitrifying bacteria act on **nitrates**; and N₂ is fixed by **bacteria** living in the roots of legumes, not by the plants themselves.

steps.text: **Fixation:** bacteria (legume nodules), lightning and the Haber process turn N₂ into NH₄⁺ or NO₃⁻.
**Nitrification:** nitrifying bacteria oxidise NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻.
**Plants and animals:** roots absorb NO₃⁻ to make proteins; animals eat plants; death and waste return NH₄⁺ via decomposers.
**Denitrification:** denitrifying bacteria turn NO₃⁻ back into N₂.

cards.title: Worked example: why farmers rotate crops with beans
cards.problem: A farmer grows chickpeas one year and wheat the next. Explain the chemistry.

steps.text: Chickpeas are legumes; their root nodules hold nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
The bacteria turn N₂ from the air into ammonium compounds that the plant uses.
When the roots and leftover plants decay, decomposers and nitrifying bacteria release ammonium and nitrates into the soil.
The wheat then uses these nitrates — less fertiliser is needed.

cards.answer: Legumes fix nitrogen and enrich the soil.

steps.text: **Step 1.** The **Ostwald process** is the industrial method used to produce nitric acid ($$ HNO_3 $$) from ammonia ($$ NH_3 $$) through catalytic oxidation.

cards.title: 3.4.1 Sulphur
body: Materials required: Sulphur, carbon disulphide, a glass rod, water, test tubes, a Bunsen burner, glass rods, a watch glass.
**What** is the colour and odour of the sulphur.
Place the sulphur into a watch glass and crash it with a glass rod.
**Sulphur** is a bright-yellow non-metallic element.

cards.title: Extraction of sulphur: the Frasch process, step by step
body: Sulphur occurs **free** in underground deposits (Italy, Mexico, Japan, Poland, USA; in Eritrea at Marsa Fatuma and Erta Ale) and **combined** in ores such as pyrite FeS₂, zinc blende ZnS, galena PbS and chalcopyrite CuFeS₂ (Debarwa, Adi Nefas). Deep deposits are hard to mine by digging (loose sand, poisonous H₂S), so the sulphur is **melted underground and pushed up**.
**Step 1 — Drill** a hole down to the deposit.
**Step 2 — Insert three pipes, one inside another** (concentric).
**Step 3 — Pump superheated water** (about 170 °C, kept liquid by high pressure) down the **outer, largest pipe**. Sulphur melts at about 115 °C, so it melts around the pipe.
**Step 4 — Blow hot compressed air** down the **inner, smallest pipe**. It mixes with the molten sulphur and makes a light **froth**.
**Step 5 — The froth of molten sulphur, water and air rises up the middle pipe** to the surface.
**Step 6 — Collect and cool** in large tanks: the sulphur solidifies, about **99.5 % pure**, so it needs no further purification.

**Why it works:** sulphur has a **low melting point** (below the temperature of superheated water), it is **insoluble in water** (so it is not washed away), and as a froth with air it is **light enough to be pushed up**.

**Sulphur from ores:** roasting sulphide ores gives SO₂ directly, which is used to make sulphuric acid: \(4\mathrm{FeS_{2}(s)} + 11\mathrm{O_{2}(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}(s)} + 8\mathrm{SO_{2}(g)}\).

cards.title: The Contact process for sulphuric acid, step by step
body: Sulphuric acid is made in larger amounts than any other chemical. The **Contact process** gives concentrated, very pure acid in high yield. Its name comes from Stage 2, where the gases react **in contact with** the surface of a solid catalyst.
**Stage 1 — Make SO₂.** Burn sulphur in dry air (or roast sulphide ores):
$$\mathrm{S(s)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{SO_{2}(g)}$$
The gas is **purified** (dust removed, dried) because impurities, especially dust and arsenic compounds, would **poison the catalyst**.
**Stage 2 — Convert SO₂ to SO₃** (the key step). The reaction is **reversible** and **exothermic**:
$$2\mathrm{SO_{2}(g)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} \overset{\mathrm{V_{2}O_{5}},\ \text{450}{}^{\circ}\text{C}}{\rightleftharpoons} 2\mathrm{SO_{3}(g)} \qquad \Delta H = -197\ \text{kJ}$$
**Conditions:** catalyst **vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅**; temperature **about 450 °C**; pressure **1–2 atm**; excess air. About 99 % conversion is reached over several catalyst beds.
**Stage 3 — Absorb SO₃** in **98 % sulphuric acid** to form **oleum** (fuming sulphuric acid):
$$\mathrm{SO_{3}(g)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_{2}S_{2}O_{7}(l)}$$
**Stage 4 — Dilute the oleum** carefully with water to give 98 % acid:
$$\mathrm{H_{2}S_{2}O_{7}(l)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(l)}$$

**Why not SO₃ straight into water?** \(\mathrm{SO_{3}(g)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(l)}\) is so exothermic that the water boils and a **fine mist** of acid droplets forms, which is hard to condense and escapes.
**Correction:** the textbook prints Stage 2 as “2SO₂ + O₂ → SO₃”; it must be **2SO₃** on the right (S: 2 = 2, O: 6 = 6) with a reversible arrow ⇌.

steps.text: **Burner:** S + O₂ → SO₂; then the gas is cleaned and dried so the catalyst is not poisoned.
**Converter:** 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ over V₂O₅ at about 450 °C, 1–2 atm.
**Absorber:** SO₃ dissolves in 98 % H₂SO₄ → oleum H₂S₂O₇.
**Diluter:** H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄; part of the acid goes back to the absorber.

cards.title: Properties of sulphuric acid, with equations
body: **Physical:** colourless, oily, dense (1.84 g/cm³ for 98 %), high boiling point (≈ 338 °C); it mixes with water giving out **a lot of heat** — **always add acid to water, slowly, never water to acid**.
**1 · Dilute acid is a strong, dibasic acid.** It turns blue litmus red and reacts with metals above hydrogen, with bases and with carbonates:
$$\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}(g)}$$
$$\mathrm{Mg(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}(g)}$$
Two H⁺ per molecule → two kinds of salt: the **normal** salt (sulphate) and the **acid** salt (hydrogensulphate):
$$2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$$
$$\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaHSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$$
**2 · Concentrated acid is a dehydrating agent** — it removes water, even the H and O atoms of compounds. Sugar turns into a black column of carbon with steam:
$$\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}(s)} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. acid}} 12\mathrm{C(s)} + 11\mathrm{H_{2}O(g)}$$
Blue copper(II) sulphate crystals turn white: \(\mathrm{CuSO_{4}\cdot 5H_{2}O(s)} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. acid}} \mathrm{CuSO_{4}(s)} + 5\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}\).
**3 · Hot concentrated acid is an oxidising agent** (it is reduced to SO₂):
$$\mathrm{Cu(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{SO_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$$
$$\mathrm{C(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{SO_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(g)}$$
$$\mathrm{S(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(l)} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{SO_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(g)}$$
**4 · It is non-volatile,** so it drives the more volatile acids out of their salts:
$$\mathrm{NaCl(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaHSO_{4}(s)} + \mathrm{HCl(g)}$$
$$\mathrm{NaNO_{3}(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaHSO_{4}(s)} + \mathrm{HNO_{3}(g)}$$
**Corrections:** sugar (sucrose) is **C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁** (the textbook prints C₁₂O₂₂H₁₁); copper and carbon each need **two** H₂SO₄ in their equations, as written above.

cards.title: Sulphates: preparation, test and uses
body: **Sulphates** are salts of sulphuric acid in which the hydrogen is replaced by a metal (or NH₄⁺). Choose the method by solubility.

**Method 1 — Acid + metal.** (a) Dilute acid with a metal above hydrogen: \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}(g)}\). (b) Hot concentrated acid with copper: \(\mathrm{Cu(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{SO_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}\).

**Method 2 — Dilute acid + oxide, hydroxide or carbonate:** \(\mathrm{CuO(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}\); \(\mathrm{MgCO_{3}(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}\).
**Method 3 — Double decomposition (precipitation)** for the insoluble sulphates BaSO₄ and PbSO₄ (CaSO₄ is only slightly soluble):
$$\mathrm{BaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{BaSO_{4}(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)}$$
$$\mathrm{Ba^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{BaSO_{4}(s)}$$

**Test for a sulphate (Activity 3.13):** add dilute HCl, then barium chloride solution. A **white precipitate** of BaSO₄ shows sulphate ions. (The HCl removes carbonate and sulphite, which would also give white precipitates.)

**Uses of sulphuric acid:** more than half goes into **fertilisers** — ammonium sulphate (NH₄)₂SO₄ and superphosphate Ca(H₂PO₄)₂ — and also into detergents, paints and pigments, fibres and plastics, as a dehydrating agent, and as the electrolyte in car (lead–acid) batteries.
**Correction:** the formula of calcium dihydrogenphosphate in superphosphate is **Ca(H₂PO₄)₂** (Ca²⁺ with two H₂PO₄⁻), not Ca(H₂PO₄)₃.

cards.problem: State the role of sulphur dioxide in (a) 2HNO₃ + SO₂ → H₂SO₄ + 2NO₂, (b) 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O.

steps.text: (a) S goes from +4 in SO₂ to +6 in H₂SO₄ — it is oxidised, so SO₂ is the **reducing agent** (HNO₃ is reduced to NO₂).
(b) S in SO₂ goes from +4 to 0 — it is reduced, so SO₂ is the **oxidising agent** (S in H₂S goes from −2 to 0).
$$2\mathrm{H_{2}S(g)} + \mathrm{SO_{2}(g)} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{S(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$$

cards.title: Step by step: Sulphur and its compounds
body: **Step 1:** Sulphur is a yellow, brittle non-metal, insoluble in water but soluble in carbon disulphide; it has allotropes (rhombic, stable below 96 °C, and monoclinic).
**Step 2:** It burns with a blue flame to form sulphur dioxide: S + O₂ → SO₂.

**Step 3:** In the laboratory SO₂ is made from sodium sulphite and dilute HCl: Na₂SO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + SO₂; it is a dense gas collected by downward delivery. SO₂ is acidic and a bleaching/reducing agent.

**Step 4:** Contact process: (1) burn S → SO₂; (2) 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ over V₂O₅ catalyst at about 450 °C and 1–2 atm; (3) absorb SO₃ in concentrated H₂SO₄ to form oleum H₂S₂O₇; (4) dilute: H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄.
**Step 5:** Concentrated H₂SO₄ is a dehydrating agent (chars sugar), an oxidising agent and a strong acid when dilute; uses include fertilizers, batteries and detergents.

**Example:** Why not dissolve SO₃ directly in water? The reaction is so exothermic that it forms a fine acid mist that is hard to collect, so SO₃ is absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ first, then diluted.

questions.q: Dry ice is made by:-

questions.q: Which of the following statements **does not** describe a property of nonmetals?

options.D: Nonmetals donate electrons to form anions.

questions.q: Which one of the following oxides dissolve in water to give a solution that has a pH of less than 7?
why:
**Step 1:** Identify the nature of the oxides. Metal oxides are generally basic, while non-metal oxides are generally acidic.
**Step 2:** Analyze the choices: 
- $$ MgO, Li_2O, K_2O, $$ and $$ Na_2O $$ are metal oxides and form basic solutions ($$ pH > 7 $$).
- $$ SO_2 $$ is a non-metal oxide.
**Step 3:** Reaction of $$ SO_2 $$ with water: $$ SO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_3 $$ (Sulfurous acid).
**Step 4:** Acids have a $$ pH < 7 $$. Therefore, Sulfur dioxide is the correct answer.
